tips.title: Neutrons are a subtraction
tips.body: **neutrons = mass number − atomic number**. The mass number counts protons and neutrons; the atomic number counts the protons. Electrons are never counted, because their mass is negligible.

tips.title: Sodium never becomes neon
tips.body: Forming Na⁺ moves an **electron**. The **11 protons** stay, and the proton number *is* the element. Its electron arrangement matches neon's, but it is still sodium — just charged.

tips.title: A relative atomic mass must land between
tips.body: It is a weighted average, so it lies **between** the lightest and heaviest isotope and **nearer the commoner one**. Chlorine's 35.5 sits between 35 and 37, nearer 35. Outside that range means an arithmetic slip.

tips.title: Outer electrons come first
tips.body: The number of outer electrons gives the **group**, and the group gives the chemistry. Sodium 2,8,**1** and potassium 2,8,8,**1** react alike because of that **1** — they are neighbours in the table as a *result*, not a cause.

tips.title: Ion charges are predictable
tips.body: Atoms form the ion that gives them a **full outer shell**. Sodium is 2,8,1, so it loses one; chlorine is 2,8,7, so it gains one. That predicts the charge instead of asking you to memorise it.

why.matters:
Almost everything chemistry does happens to **electrons**, and mostly to the outer ones. The nucleus settles what the element is and how heavy it is, and then takes no further part — no chemical reaction has ever changed one.

That single split explains two things at once. **Isotopes** of an element behave identically, because they differ only in the part that does no chemistry. And an **ion** is not a small adjustment to an atom: moving one electron turns a metal that catches fire on water into the crystals on the table.

examples.title: Why table salt is safe
examples.body:
Sodium is a metal soft enough to cut with a knife, and it catches fire on water. Chlorine is a choking green gas. Put them together and you get the crystals you shake onto chips.

No nucleus changed. Each sodium atom (2,8,1) hands its outer electron to a chlorine atom (2,8,7), leaving Na⁺ (2,8) and Cl⁻ (2,8,8) — both with a full outer shell and so no reason to react with anything. The danger in the elements was the outer electron, and in salt that electron has already found a home.

visual.alt: A dot and cross diagram showing sodium’s single outer electron moving across to chlorine, leaving a sodium ion with a full shell of eight and a chloride ion with a full shell of eight

examples.title: The three protons between lead and gold
examples.body:
Alchemists spent centuries trying to turn lead into gold, and one line of this topic says why they could not. The number of protons **is** the element: lead has 82, gold has 79, and no chemical reaction moves a proton. Chemistry rearranges electrons and nothing else.

So gold has to be dug up, and a gold-plated ring is a genuine thin layer of gold on a cheaper metal underneath. Changing one element into another is possible, but only by meddling with the nucleus in a reactor — which is not chemistry at all.

props.caption: Three protons apart, and no chemistry can move one

visual.alt: Three bars of almost identical length showing the proton numbers of gold at seventy-nine, mercury at eighty and lead at eighty-two, the small difference that no chemical reaction can change

examples.title: Heavy water, and the ice cube that sinks
examples.body:
Hydrogen has an isotope with a neutron in it, and water built from that isotope is chemically ordinary water: same formula, same reactions, because the electrons are the same. But each molecule has a relative formula mass of **20** rather than **18**, and the liquid is about a tenth denser.

That extra mass shows itself in one striking way. Ice made from heavy water **sinks** in ordinary water, while ordinary ice floats. Neutrons add mass and nothing else — and here is the mass, doing the only thing mass can do.

visual.alt: A table comparing ordinary water and heavy water: the same kind of formula, relative masses of eighteen against twenty, densities of 0.997 against 1.105 grams per cubic centimetre, and ice that floats against ice that sinks

steps.title: Atoms, elements and compounds
steps.body:
**All substances are made of atoms.** An **atom** is the **smallest part of an element that can exist**.

- Atoms of each element are represented by a **chemical symbol** — O for an atom of oxygen, Na for an atom of sodium.
- There are about **100 different elements**, shown in the **periodic table**.
- **Compounds** are formed from elements by **chemical reactions**.
- A chemical reaction always involves **the formation of one or more new substances**, and often a detectable **energy change**.
- Compounds contain **two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions**, and are represented by **formulae**.
- **Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.**

**That last point is the one that separates a compound from a mixture.** Water is a compound: hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined, in fixed proportions, and no amount of filtering or distilling will separate them — it takes a chemical reaction, such as electrolysis. Air is a **mixture**: the gases are not chemically combined, and they **can** be separated by a physical process such as fractional distillation.

**Fixed proportions** matters too. Water is always $\mathrm{H_2O}$ — two hydrogens to one oxygen, every time. A mixture can be in any proportion at all, which is why you can make tea stronger or weaker but cannot make water *more* watery.

by a physical process, such as filtration or distillation

steps.title: Naming compounds from formulae
steps.body:
**The periodic table is given to you in the exam, so the symbols are there to look up. The names of compounds are not.** You should be able to name a compound from its formula, or from a symbol equation, and write word equations from them.

That needs the names and symbols of the **first 20 elements**, of **Groups 1 and 7**, and of the other elements in the course, such as copper, iron and zinc. Everything else follows from a few rules.

**Rule 1: the metal comes first, unchanged.** In NaCl the sodium stays **sodium**.

**Rule 2: two elements only, the second ends in -ide.** Chlorine becomes chlor**ide**, oxygen becomes ox**ide**, sulfur becomes sulf**ide**, bromine becomes brom**ide**.

- NaCl is sodium chloride. MgO is magnesium oxide. K₂S is potassium sulfide.

**Rule 3: a group containing oxygen ends in -ate.** Three groups of atoms stay together in many reactions and have their own names:

- SO₄ is **sulfate**, so CuSO₄ is copper sulfate.
- NO₃ is **nitrate**, so KNO₃ is potassium nitrate.
- CO₃ is **carbonate**, so CaCO₃ is calcium carbonate.

The ending is the clue. **-ide** means just the element, and **-ate** means the element **with oxygen**. So CaS is calcium sulfide, but CaSO₄ is calcium sulfate. Calling CaCO₃ "calcium carbide" or "calcium carbon oxide" loses the mark.

**Two groups you learn as names.** OH is **hydroxide**, so NaOH is sodium hydroxide; it ends in -ide even though it contains oxygen. NH₄ is **ammonium**, and it goes **first**, where a metal would: NH₄Cl is ammonium chloride, and the fertiliser (NH₄)₂SO₄ is ammonium sulfate.

**Two non-metals: count with prefixes.** **Mono-** means one and **di-** means two. CO is carbon **mon**oxide, CO₂ is carbon **di**oxide, SO₂ is sulfur dioxide and NO₂ is nitrogen dioxide.

**Iron and copper can form more than one ion,** so you may see a Roman numeral in their name too, such as iron(II) chloride.

**Some names you just learn.** H₂O is water, NH₃ is ammonia and CH₄ is methane. HCl is hydrochloric acid, H₂SO₄ is sulfuric acid and HNO₃ is nitric acid. An element written as a pair of atoms, such as H₂, O₂ or Cl₂, keeps its plain name: **hydrogen**, not "dihydrogen".

**From a symbol equation.** Name each substance in turn:

$$\mathrm{Mg + 2HCl \rightarrow MgCl_2 + H_2}$$

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. The big numbers in front do not appear in a word equation, and neither do the small ones inside a formula: MgCl₂ is magnesium chloride, not "magnesium dichloride".

steps.title: The three subatomic particles
steps.body:
An atom has a **nucleus** containing **protons** and **neutrons**, with **electrons** in shells around it.

**The relative charges and masses:**


**In an atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons**, so the +1 charges and the −1 charges cancel exactly and **atoms have no overall electrical charge**.

**The atomic number is the number of protons.** Two facts follow, and both are asked about:

- **All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.**
- **Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.**

So the proton number *is* the element's identity. Change it and you have a different element — which is why you cannot turn lead into gold with a chemical reaction; chemistry only rearranges electrons.

**The mass number is the sum of the protons and neutrons.** Electrons are not counted, because their mass is so small it makes no difference.

$$\textbf{neutrons} = \textbf{mass number} - \textbf{atomic number}$$

check.solution: $35 - 17 = 18$ neutrons. The mass number counts protons **and** neutrons, so subtracting the protons leaves the neutrons.

steps.title: How small, and where the mass is
steps.body:
**Atoms are very small.** The spec gives figures you are expected to know and use:

- An atom has a radius of about **0.1 nm**, which is $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
- The radius of a **nucleus** is **less than 1/10 000** of that of the atom — about $1 \times 10^{-14}$ m.
- **Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.**

**Put those two facts together and you get the picture that matters.** The nucleus holds nearly all the mass in a space **ten thousand times smaller** in radius than the atom. So an atom is **overwhelmingly empty space**, with something extraordinarily dense at its centre.

That is worth a moment, because it is the result that overturned the plum pudding model — and it is also the third limitation of the simple particle model, where atoms are drawn as **solid** spheres.

**A sense of the scale.** If an atom were the size of a sports stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea at the centre. Everything else is electrons and space.

**Using the prefix nano.** *Nano* means $10^{-9}$, so 0.1 nm $= 0.1 \times 10^{-9}$ m $= 1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. Moving between nanometres and metres is a skill the spec asks for by name, and it is where the marks go in this part.

steps.title: Isotopes
steps.body:
**Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These atoms are called isotopes of that element.**

The number of **protons** is fixed by the element — change it and it is no longer the same element. The number of **neutrons** can vary.

**Chlorine is the standard example:**

- **Chlorine-35** — 17 protons, **18** neutrons
- **Chlorine-37** — 17 protons, **20** neutrons

Both are chlorine, because both have 17 protons. They differ by **two neutrons**, and so by two in mass number.

**Isotopes have the same chemical properties.** This is worth understanding rather than memorising: chemical behaviour is decided by **electrons**, and specifically by the **outer electrons**. Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons, so the same number of electrons, so the same electronic structure — so they react identically. The extra neutrons change the **mass** and nothing about the chemistry.

**Writing an isotope.** The mass number goes at the top left and the atomic number at the bottom left of the symbol, so chlorine-37 is written with 37 above 17. In plain text it is usually written **chlorine-37**, and that name tells you the **mass number**.

**The quick calculation:** given the two numbers, protons = atomic number, electrons = the same again in a neutral atom, and neutrons = mass number − atomic number.

steps.title: Relative atomic mass from abundance
steps.body:
**The relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.**

That is why relative atomic masses are rarely whole numbers: chlorine's is **35.5**, not because any chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5, but because chlorine is a mixture of two isotopes and 35.5 is their weighted average.

visuals.problem: Chlorine is 75% chlorine-35 and 25% chlorine-37. Calculate its relative atomic mass.

steps.text: Multiply each mass number by its percentage abundance

so the relative atomic mass is 35.5
because chlorine-35 is the commoner isotope, the average is pulled towards it

steps.title: Electronic structure
steps.body:
**The electrons in an atom occupy the lowest available energy levels** — the innermost available shells. Electrons fill from the inside out.

**For the first twenty elements the shells hold 2, then 8, then 8, then 2.** You are expected to be able to represent the electronic structures of **the first twenty elements** in both forms: as **numbers** and as a **diagram**.

**Sodium** has 11 electrons, so its electronic structure is **2,8,1** — two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second and one in the third.

**Worked through:**

- **Oxygen**, 8 electrons: 2 in the first shell, 6 in the second → **2,6**
- **Chlorine**, 17 electrons: 2, then 8, then 7 → **2,8,7**
- **Argon**, 18 electrons: 2, 8, 8 → **2,8,8** — every shell full
- **Potassium**, 19 electrons: 2, 8, 8, then 1 → **2,8,8,1**
- **Calcium**, 20 electrons: **2,8,8,2**

**You may answer in terms of either energy levels or shells** — the spec accepts both words.

**Why this is the most useful thing in the topic.** The number of electrons in the **outer shell** decides the element's **group**, and therefore its chemistry. Sodium is 2,8,**1** and potassium is 2,8,8,**1**: both have one outer electron, both are in **Group 1**, and both react in the same way. Chlorine is 2,8,**7** — seven outer electrons, **Group 7**. Argon's outer shell is full, so it is unreactive and sits in **Group 0**.

That single link — **outer electrons decide the group, and the group decides the chemistry** — is what the whole periodic table rests on.

props.title: The number of outer electrons gives the group, and the group gives the chemistry

visuals.alt: A table of electronic structures worked out by filling the shells from the inside out

steps.title: Ions
steps.body:
An **ion** is an atom, or group of atoms, that has **gained or lost electrons** and therefore has an **overall electrical charge**.

**Only electrons move.** The protons stay put — they are in the nucleus, and changing them would change the element. So:

- **Lose** electrons → **fewer** negatives than positives → a **positive** ion
- **Gain** electrons → **more** negatives than positives → a **negative** ion

$$\textbf{charge} = \textbf{protons} - \textbf{electrons}$$

**Worked through:**

- **Na⁺** — sodium has 11 protons. The ion has a 1+ charge, so it has **10** electrons: it has **lost one**.
- **Cl⁻** — chlorine has 17 protons. The ion has a 1− charge, so it has **18** electrons: it has **gained one**.
- **O²⁻** — oxygen has 8 protons. The ion has a 2− charge, so it has **10** electrons: it has **gained two**.

**Why those particular charges?** Because of the electronic structure. Sodium is 2,8,1 — losing its single outer electron leaves 2,8, a full outer shell. Chlorine is 2,8,7 — gaining one gives 2,8,8, also full. **Atoms form ions that give them a full outer shell**, which is the arrangement of the nearest noble gas.

**Notice what that means.** Na⁺ and O²⁻ both end up with **10** electrons, the same as neon. They are chemically nothing like neon, because they still have their own number of protons — but their electron arrangement matches.

**The mistake to avoid:** saying that sodium *becomes* neon. It does not. It has 11 protons and always will; only its electrons have changed.

props.title: Only electrons move; the protons never change, so the element never changes

visuals.alt: A table of three common ions, showing which electrons have moved and why

check.prompt: A magnesium ion is written Mg2+. Magnesium has an atomic number of 12. How many electrons does the ion have?
check.solution: $12 - 2 = 10$ electrons. It has **lost two**, leaving 2,8 — a full outer shell.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**The proton number is the element's identity.** All atoms of an element have the same number of protons; atoms of different elements have different numbers. So a chemical reaction can never change one element into another — chemistry only rearranges **electrons**. That is why *sodium becomes neon* is wrong: sodium loses an electron and keeps its eleven protons, so it is still sodium, just charged.

**Isotopes: same chemistry, different mass — and be able to say why.** The reason is that chemical behaviour depends on **electrons**, and isotopes have the same number of protons and therefore the same number of electrons and the same electronic structure. Neutrons contribute mass and nothing else. An answer that states the fact earns less than one that gives that reason.

**Relative atomic mass is an average, so check it lands in the right place.** It must lie **between** the lightest and heaviest isotope, and **nearer the commoner one**. Chlorine's 35.5 is between 35 and 37 and nearer 35, because chlorine-35 is three times as common. If your answer falls outside that range you have divided by the wrong thing; if it is on the wrong side of the middle you have swapped the abundances.

**An atom is mostly empty space, and the two figures prove it.** Nearly all the mass sits in a nucleus whose radius is **less than one ten-thousandth** of the atom's. Quoting both figures together is what earns the second mark, because one alone does not establish it.

**Outer electrons decide everything.** The group number follows from the outer shell; the chemistry follows from the group. Sodium 2,8,**1** and potassium 2,8,8,**1** react alike because both have one outer electron — not because they are near each other on the table, which is the effect rather than the cause. Getting that the right way round is a genuine Higher-tier distinction.

**Why ions have the charges they do.** Atoms form ions that give them a **full outer shell**, matching the nearest noble gas. Sodium loses one to reach 2,8; chlorine gains one to reach 2,8,8. This predicts the charges rather than requiring you to remember them, which matters when you meet an unfamiliar element.

**The nano prefix is where calculation marks go.** *Nano* is $10^{-9}$, so 0.1 nm is $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m. The physics is easy and the index arithmetic is where answers go wrong — so convert first and write the power of ten down before doing anything else.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- An **atom** is the **smallest part of an element that can exist**. There are about **100 elements**.
- **Compounds**: two or more elements **chemically combined in fixed proportions**, separable **only by a chemical reaction**.
- **Naming**: metal first; two elements end in **-ide**; a group with oxygen ends in **-ate** (sulfate, nitrate, carbonate); OH is **hydroxide**, NH₄ is **ammonium**.
- **Proton**: charge **+1**, mass **1**, in the nucleus. **Neutron**: **0**, mass **1**, in the nucleus. **Electron**: **−1**, **very small** mass, in shells.
- Electrons **equal** protons in an atom, so an atom has **no overall charge**.
- **Atomic number = protons**, and it is the element's identity.
- **Mass number = protons + neutrons.** So **neutrons = mass number − atomic number**.
- An atom's radius is about **0.1 nm**, or $1 \times 10^{-10}$ m.
- The nucleus is **less than 1/10 000** of that radius, about $1 \times 10^{-14}$ m, and holds **almost all the mass**.
- So an atom is **mostly empty space**.
- **Isotopes**: atoms of the same element with **different numbers of neutrons**.
- Isotopes have **identical chemical properties**, because they have the **same electrons**.
- **Relative atomic mass** is an **average weighted by abundance** — which is why it is rarely a whole number.
- Electrons fill the **lowest available energy levels**; for the first twenty elements the shells hold **2, 8, 8, 2**.
- Sodium is **2,8,1**. You should know the first **twenty** elements, as numbers and as diagrams.
- The number of **outer electrons** gives the **group**, and the group gives the chemistry.
- An **ion** has gained or lost **electrons**: **charge = protons − electrons**.
- Atoms form ions that give them a **full outer shell**.

questions.prompt: Why does chlorine form a 1- ion rather than a 1+ ion?
questions.solution: Chlorine is 2,8,**7**. **Gaining one** electron gives 2,8,8 — a **full outer shell**, matching the nearest noble gas. Atoms form the ion that reaches a full shell most easily, which predicts the charge rather than requiring you to remember it.

questions.prompt: Explain what isotopes are, why they have identical chemical properties, and why relative atomic masses are often not whole numbers.
questions.solution: Isotopes are atoms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons. The number of protons is fixed by the element and cannot change without changing the element itself, but the number of neutrons may vary. Chlorine, for example, exists as chlorine-35, which has seventeen protons and eighteen neutrons, and as chlorine-37, which has seventeen protons and twenty neutrons. Both are chlorine because both have seventeen protons, and they differ by two neutrons and therefore by two in their mass numbers. Isotopes of an element have identical chemical properties because chemical behaviour is determined by electrons, and in particular by the electrons in the outer shell. Since isotopes have the same number of protons, a neutral atom of each has the same number of electrons and therefore the same electronic structure, so they react in exactly the same way. The additional neutrons contribute mass to the nucleus but take no part in bonding, so they affect physical properties such as density slightly but do not affect the chemistry at all. Relative atomic masses are often not whole numbers because the relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of each of its isotopes. Chlorine is about seventy five per cent chlorine-35 and twenty five per cent chlorine-37, so its relative atomic mass is calculated as seventy five times thirty five plus twenty five times thirty seven, all divided by one hundred, which gives 35.5. No individual chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5; the value is a weighted mean, and it lies between the two mass numbers and nearer to that of the more abundant isotope.

questions.modelAnswer:
**What isotopes are.** Atoms of the **same element** with **different numbers of neutrons**. The protons are fixed by the element; the neutrons may vary.

**Example.** Chlorine-35 has 17 protons and **18** neutrons; chlorine-37 has 17 protons and **20** neutrons. Both are chlorine because both have **17 protons**.

**Why the chemistry is identical.** Chemical behaviour is determined by **electrons**, especially the outer ones. Same protons → same electrons → **same electronic structure** → identical reactions. The extra neutrons add **mass** and take no part in bonding.

**Why relative atomic masses are not whole numbers.** Relative atomic mass is an **average weighted by abundance**:

$$\frac{(75 \times 35) + (25 \times 37)}{100} = \frac{3550}{100} = 35.5$$

**No chlorine atom has a mass of 35.5.** It is a weighted mean — which is why it lies **between** 35 and 37 and **nearer 35**, the commoner isotope. Checking that is a free check on any answer of this kind.

questions.prompt: Explain how the electronic structure of an atom determines its position in the periodic table and the ion it forms. Use sodium and chlorine as examples.
questions.solution: Electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels, filling the innermost shells first, and for the first twenty elements the shells hold two, then eight, then eight, then two. Sodium has eleven electrons, so its electronic structure is 2,8,1, and chlorine has seventeen, so its structure is 2,8,7. The number of occupied shells gives the period, and the number of electrons in the outer shell gives the group, so sodium is in Group 1 and chlorine is in Group 7. This matters because the outer electrons are the ones involved in bonding, so elements with the same number of outer electrons have similar chemical properties, which is exactly why the periodic table places them in the same column. It is worth being clear about the direction of the reasoning: sodium and potassium do not react alike because they sit near one another in the table, but rather they are placed in the same column because they react alike, and they react alike because each has one outer electron. The electronic structure also predicts the ion each atom forms, because atoms form ions that give them a full outer shell, matching the arrangement of the nearest noble gas. Sodium has a single outer electron, so losing it leaves 2,8, a full outer shell, and the ion formed is Na+ with eleven protons and ten electrons. Chlorine has seven outer electrons, so gaining one gives 2,8,8, also full, and the ion formed is Cl− with seventeen protons and eighteen electrons. In each case only electrons move; the number of protons is unchanged, so the element is unchanged.

criteria.text: Links outer electrons to the group

questions.modelAnswer:
**Filling the shells.** Electrons occupy the **lowest available energy levels**; for the first twenty elements the shells hold **2, 8, 8, 2**. Sodium (11 electrons) is **2,8,1**; chlorine (17) is **2,8,7**.

**Position in the table.** The number of **occupied shells** gives the **period**; the number of **outer electrons** gives the **group**. So sodium is **Group 1** and chlorine is **Group 7**.

**And the reasoning runs this way round**, which is the point worth making: sodium and potassium are **placed in the same column because they react alike**, and they react alike **because each has one outer electron**. Not the reverse.

**The ion each forms.** Atoms form the ion that gives them a **full outer shell**, matching the nearest noble gas:

- **Sodium** loses its one outer electron → 2,8 → **Na⁺**, 11 protons and 10 electrons.
- **Chlorine** gains one → 2,8,8 → **Cl⁻**, 17 protons and 18 electrons.

**In both cases only electrons move.** The proton number is unchanged, so the **element** is unchanged — sodium ions are still sodium.

questions.prompt: Name the compound with the formula MgO.
questions.solution: **Magnesium oxide.** Magnesium is the metal, so it comes first; only two elements, so oxygen becomes **oxide**.

questions.prompt: Name the compound with the formula K₂SO₄.
questions.solution: **Potassium sulfate.** SO₄ is the sulfate group, and the 2 does not appear in the name: it only says two potassium ions balance one sulfate.

markScheme.description: potassium sulfate

questions.prompt: Zinc reacts with sulfuric acid: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂. A student writes the word equation as zinc + sulfuric acid → zinc sulfide + hydrogen. What is wrong?
questions.solution: **-ide** means the element on its own, as in zinc sulfide, ZnS. ZnSO₄ has the **sulfate** group, sulfur **with oxygen**, so it is **zinc sulfate**. H₂ keeps its plain name, hydrogen, and the small numbers never appear in a name.

markScheme.description: zinc sulfate, because SO₄ contains oxygen

options: Zinc should come second, because the acid is always named first in a word equation
Hydrogen should be written dihydrogen, because it is H₂
ZnSO₄ contains oxygen in the SO₄ group, so it is zinc sulfate
The 4 in SO₄ means it should be zinc tetrasulfide

examTechnique.body:
Find neutrons by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number.

Remember that in an atom the electrons equal the protons, but in an ion they do not.

Explain isotopes by saying that chemistry depends on electrons, not just that they have the same properties.

Check a relative atomic mass lies between the isotope masses and nearer the commoner one.

Fill electron shells from the inside out, using 2, 8, 8, 2 for the first twenty elements.

Give the group from the number of outer electrons.

Explain an ion's charge by the full outer shell it reaches.

Convert nanometres to metres before any calculation, and write the power of ten down first.

Name a compound metal first, with **-ide** for two elements and **-ate** for a group containing oxygen, and leave the numbers out of the name.
examinerErrors: Adding the atomic number to the mass number instead of subtracting.
Giving an ion the same number of electrons as protons.
Saying sodium becomes neon when it forms Na+.
Stating that isotopes have the same chemistry without giving the electron reason.
Treating relative atomic mass as a whole number.
Filling the third shell with more than eight electrons for the first twenty elements.
Saying elements react alike because they are near each other in the table.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer treats the proton number as the element's identity, so it never claims a reaction changes one element into another. It explains isotopes through electrons rather than asserting the result, and it checks a relative atomic mass against the range it must fall in. It builds an electronic structure by filling shells rather than recalling it, reads the group off the outer shell, and predicts an ion's charge from the full shell it reaches. And it gets the direction of the argument right: elements share a column because they share an outer-shell count, not the other way round.
